scope: First-person works — autobiographies, prison writings, and court chronicles in which Indians wrote themselves into the historical record. Cross-cuts every era from Babur to independence.

collections.title: First-person works of the subcontinent
collections.subtitle: Autobiographies, prison writings, and court chronicles in which Indians wrote themselves into the record.
collections.summary: Babur opens the Baburnama with his father's death; Nehru opens The Discovery of India with his arrest. Across five centuries Indians have used first-person prose — memoir, chronicle, prison notebook — to argue for who they were and what India was. The corpus tags each as memoir; this collection gathers them.
collections.framing: First-person texts have a load-bearing role in subcontinental history that translation traditions sometimes obscure. The Baburnama is the only surviving Timurid royal autobiography in any language. The Akbarnama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, and Padshahnama together form a continuous Mughal court chronicle from 1556 to 1658. Three centuries later the prison writings of Gandhi, Nehru, and Ambedkar — drafted in Yerwada, Ahmednagar, and various Bombay jails — became the founding texts of the Indian republic's self-conception. To gather them in one place is to put the writer-rulers of the sixteenth century in conversation with the writer-prisoners of the twentieth. Tag any new entry with \"memoir\" and it joins automatically.
